fallback_summary_en: Languages organize nouns and agreement in very different ways. Some have no grammatical noun gender, some have two or three genders, and some use larger noun-class systems. Articles can make gender visible, but article count is not the same thing as gender count.

transparency_slide.description: The lesson compares grammatical gender systems without assuming every language has gender, articles, or a masculine/feminine/neuter three-way split.
transparency_slide.rendering_model: Build one ordered language array from relevant profile/session languages. If no genderless profile is present, add English. If no two-gender profile is present, add Spanish. If no three-gender profile is present, add Greek. Render the system summary and representative markers with the same universal comparison components. Do not derive gender count from the number of article spellings.

support_selection.full: Render the comparison, structured rules, reviewed examples, and defensible practice for this language.
support_selection.comparison_only: Render only the reviewed gender-system comparison record. Do not invent agreement rules or practice.
support_selection.unavailable: Omit the language from this lesson until a reviewed comparison record exists.

title_policy.notes: The title names the grammatical concept, not a guessed article equivalent. Languages without articles or grammatical gender still fit the same lesson family.

eligibility.notes: English, Spanish, and Greek are conditional contrast fallbacks for zero-, two-, and three-gender systems. A noun-class language may also appear when selected, but must not be squeezed into masculine/feminine/neuter labels.

block_plan.notes: Introduce grammatical gender as a noun/agreement system. Explicitly distinguish grammatical gender from a person's gender and from biological sex.

Resolve lessons/mul/grammatical-gender/gender-examples.json. Show gender-system type plus representative article/determiner markers where the language has them. Article spellings are examples, never the definition of the system.
Use the same ordered language set. Explicitly allow no-gender, two-gender, three-gender, and noun-class comparison records.
Explain that gender may be visible on articles, adjectives, pronouns, numerals, case forms, or other agreement targets, and some languages have no grammatical gender at all.

For Spanish, teach two noun genders, article/adjective agreement, reliable-vs-unreliable ending clues, and limited neuter constructions. Never present Spanish neuter forms as a third ordinary noun gender.
Prefer lesson-safe reviewed sentences that make agreement visible. Corpus evidence remains in gef-content.
Transition from identifying the noun's gender to choosing agreement forms. Omit if no full-support learning language is selected.
Use shared cloze/feature primitives. Spanish practice may choose el/la, un/una, or a gender-variable adjective only when the noun and answer are unambiguous.
Offer a reader hunt for noun phrases whose articles/adjectives reveal grammatical gender. Do not ask learners to infer a person's gender from grammar.
Reinforce: learn the noun with its agreement pattern; endings are clues, not laws; neuter behavior differs by language.

learning_path_policy.notes: Spanish can place this early because noun/article agreement is foundational. Other languages need independent placement and may use comparison-only mode.
